name: Ser Aldric Vane
appearance: Thirty-four, beautiful in a severe way. Of the two boys who once held other men's horses together he is the one with the better seat and the better manners, and at Harrow Ford he sat his horse at Darrow's left hand, close enough to touch, with his eyes on the far bank; told he looked like a man at his own wedding, he didn't smile. He spends few words, and those courtly, patient and sincere. The last Darrow saw of him was his back, bent low over his horse's neck as it climbed the west bank out of the Wend.
last_seen_doing: Bent low over his horse's neck on the west bank of the Wend, the horse already turned and already climbing out, as Darrow went under midriver; by Darrow's count, one heartbeat early.
now: Offstage since Harrow Ford. He was last known on the west bank of the Wend with the Second Lance, which sat its horses in perfect order, untouched, watching the river carry the Ninth downstream. Seven weeks after the Binding, with six grey cloaks and a censer on the Holloway and Darrow's name first on their list, Darrow believes that a man who has ridden knee to knee with him since they were boys sat in a warm room in Calden and wrote that name; Wren said only that there was a list, and that Darrow was first on it.
story_so_far: He and Darrow were squires together, holding other men's horses, and were knighted on the same morning in the same cold chapel with their palms on the same warming stone. At Harrow Ford he had the Second Lance, held in reserve by the writ from command, and sat at Darrow's left hand on the west bank watching the far shore, telling him to ride wide, and then wider, with some other word left unsaid in his open mouth when the chaplain's bell cut him off. When the Grace went out of the Ninth midriver and Darrow went under, the last thing Darrow saw through the spray was Aldric's horse on the west bank, already turned, already climbing out, Aldric bent low over its neck; when the red-handed woman turned his head back to the water, the Second sat its horses in perfect order, untouched, watching. Seven weeks after the Binding, with grey cloaks on the Holloway and his own name first on their list, Darrow thought of a man who had ridden knee to knee with him since they were boys, in a warm room in Calden, writing that name, and heard again: Ride wide today.

known_facts.fact: He has the Second Lance, which the writ from command held in reserve while the Sixth and the Ninth cleared the ford, and he sat his horse at Darrow's left hand, close enough to touch, on the west bank of Harrow Ford.

He and Darrow rode knee to knee from the time they were squires holding other men's horses, and were knighted on the same morning in the same cold chapel, kneeling shoulder to shoulder with their palms on the Oathstone while it warmed under their hands.
Darrow still remembers his face when the Grace went into him the first time: like a man hearing music he had only ever been told about.
By Darrow's account he has the better seat, the better manners and the better luck with the kind of women whose fathers mattered.

Before the crossing he watched the far bank without smiling and told Darrow to ride wide, then wider; his mouth was open on some other word when the chaplain's bell began down the line, and he shut it and looked away.

As Darrow went under, he saw Aldric's horse on the west bank already turned and already climbing out, Aldric bent low over its neck, one heartbeat early by Darrow's count; when the red-handed woman turned Darrow's head to the river, the Second Lance sat its horses on the west bank in perfect order, untouched, watching.

On the night Maelis offered Darrow the two ways off the mountain, he thought of the field-stone warming under his palm and of Aldric's horse on the west bank, already turned, before he asked whether he could kneel after.

With Darrow's name first on the list the Confessors read out at the inn in Coldmere, Darrow believes it was written in a warm room in Calden by a man who has ridden knee to knee with him since they were boys, and hears again the words "Ride wide today."

relationships.label: sworn brother
relationships.note: They were squires together holding other men's horses and were knighted the same morning in the same cold chapel, kneeling shoulder to shoulder with their palms on the Oathstone; at the ford he sat at Darrow's left hand and told him to ride wide, and the last thing Darrow saw before the river took him was Aldric's horse on the west bank, already turned.

deeper: The Grace in him is full, and it is not his.
